titleStmt.title: The effects of prime visibility on ERP measures of masked priming
titleStmt.author: Holcomb
Reder
Misra
Grainger

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: The effects of prime visibility on ERP measures of masked priming

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Taken together, these findings provide strong evidence that the N400 repetition effects at 40 ms in this experiment were due in large part to automatic unconscious processes and were not strictly the result of conscious leakage from consciously perceived primes.

span.label: masked priming and the N400
span.quote: In these studies, the prime stimulus is presented very briefly and is then immediately obscured by either a pattern mask (e.g., a series of letters or symbols occupying the same location on the screen as the prime) or the target word itself.

span.label: eeg-erp
span.quote: In two experiments, the effect of the duration (40, 80 and 120 ms) of pattern masked prime words on subsequent target word processing was measured using event-related potentials.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Form information is extracted from the prime automatically while semantic extraction consumes capacity-limited attentional resources, so prime visibility gates semantic but not repetition priming
span.quote: The complete pattern of priming effects obtained in the present study can be explained if one assumes that form information can be extracted automatically (i.e., without attention-demanding resources), while the extraction of semantic information is either not automatic at all and depends on the allocation of capacity-limited resources or relies to a greater extent on capacity-limited resources.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repetition priming works by pre-activating shared representations whereas semantic priming works by establishing post-target connections between related representations, the latter requiring attention
span.quote: One way to avoid this relatively ad-hoc assumption would be to argue that the critical difference between repetition and semantic priming is that repetition priming is driven primarily by the pre-activation of representations that are shared by prime and target, while semantic priming involves, to a greater extent, establishing connections across related representations (e.g., as in theories such as compound-cue [ 26 ]).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The N400 indexes a resonance process at a form–meaning interface in which prime-derived form or meaning information helps the lexical processor settle on one form–meaning association
span.quote: Improving the processing of either form or meaning will help the lexical processor settle on a single form–meaning association via a resonance process involving the activation of similar form and similar meaning representations.

span.label: The 40 ms condition is acknowledged to be partly contaminated by trials on which the prime was consciously perceived.
span.quote: We acknowledge that our results in the 40 ms condition are undoubtedly contaminated to some degree by conscious leakage (18% of masked animal probes were correctly detected, suggesting that participants could sometimes consciously process primes at 40 ms).

span.label: Conscious leakage can never be fully eliminated by shortening prime duration.
span.quote: In fact, we believe it is impossible to completely eliminate this possibility, as to do so would most likely require the utilization of primes of such short duration that all priming effects would likely be precluded (no one argues that there is a lower limit past which no perceptual processing can take place!).

span.label: The data do not show that the process the N400 reflects is itself exclusively automatic, only that it is sensitive to automatic priming.
span.quote: It is important to note, however, that contrary to the claims of Deacon and others, neither we (nor they) have demonstrated that the process directly reflected by the N400 is exclusively automatic.

span.label: The columnar analysis strategy multiplies the number of statistical comparisons.
span.quote: Although this approach does increase the number of comparisons, this is offset by both a more complete description of the data and by a cautious interpretation of analyses where only a single column produces a significant effect.

span.label: four participants were excluded, three for excessive artifact and one for experimenter error
span.note: eliminates: that the averaged waveform is dominated by a few contaminated recordings
span.quote: We excluded four of these participants due to excessive artifact (three) and experimenter error (one).

span.label: response hand was counterbalanced across participants
span.note: eliminates: that a lateralised effect is a motor effect of the responding hand
span.quote: As in Experiment 1, the animal names served as probe items in a go/no-go semantic categorization task and response hand was counterbalanced.

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: If we further hypothesize that it is precisely the allocation of attention-demanding resources that determines the level of visibility of prime stimuli, then we can explain why prime visibility correlated highly with semantic priming and not with repetition priming

span.label: semantic priming
span.quote: So, unlike repetition priming in Experiment 1, for semantic priming in Experiment 2, visibility of primes at 40 ms (as measured by button presses to probe items) predicted the N400 effect for targets following very briefly presented primes

span.label: prime visibility
span.quote: If we further hypothesize that it is precisely the allocation of attention-demanding resources that determines the level of visibility of prime stimuli, then we can explain why prime visibility correlated highly with semantic priming and not with repetition priming

span.label: conscious leakage
span.quote: One question that dogs all subliminal priming studies is the issue of whether the obtained effects may be due to residual conscious processing of the primes on some percentage of the trials (a phenomena we will call “conscious leakage”)

span.label: N400
span.quote: What we have shown is that the N400 process is sensitive to the influence of automatic priming

span.label: pre-activation
span.quote: One way to avoid this relatively ad-hoc assumption would be to argue that the critical difference between repetition and semantic priming is that repetition priming is driven primarily by the pre-activation of representations that are shared by prime and target, while semantic priming involves, to a greater extent, establishing connections across related representations

span.label: THE DISSOCIATION IS MADE OF CORRELATIONS, NOT OF MEANS, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN. One measure (the N400), one design, two kinds of priming, and the question is whether each effect's size tracks how well the individual participant could see the prime: `unlike repetition priming in Experiment 1, for semantic priming in Experiment 2, VISIBILITY OF PRIMES AT 40 MS ... PREDICTED THE N400 EFFECT`. Individual differences are the instrument - a median split on d-prime - so the NULL in Experiment 1 is the informative half, not the weak one. It is also the paper's defence against its own worst confound: if repetition priming ran on conscious leakage, the participants who leaked more would prime more, and they do not
span.quote: So, unlike repetition priming in Experiment 1, for semantic priming in Experiment 2, visibility of primes at 40 ms (as measured by button presses to probe items) predicted the N400 effect for targets following very briefly presented primes

span.label: THE AUTOMATIC/CONTROLLED LINE MOVES OFF THE REPRESENTATION AND ONTO THE MECHANISM: `IT IS NOT THE TYPE OF REPRESENTATION (form or meaning) that determines the automaticity of priming effects, BUT RATHER THE TYPE OF MECHANISM utilized (pre-activation versus establishing connections).` The older account - form is automatic, meaning is not - would have to say the repetition effect is mostly form, and the authors call that assumption AD HOC in their own words rather than defending it. What replaces it is a distinction between raising the activation of a shared representation and building a link between two different ones, and only the second needs attention
span.quote: One way to avoid this relatively ad-hoc assumption would be to argue that the critical difference between repetition and semantic priming is that repetition priming is driven primarily by the pre-activation of representations that are shared by prime and target, while semantic priming involves, to a greater extent, establishing connections across related representations (e.g., as in theories such as compound-cue [ 26 ]). In this account, it is not the type of representation (form or meaning) that determines the automaticity of priming effects, but rather the type of mechanism utilized (pre-activation versus establishing connections)

span.label: THEY NAME THE RESULT THAT WOULD REFUTE THEM, which almost nothing else in this corpus does: `finding evidence of N400 priming effects on masked TARGETS would strengthen the case for the N400 being a direct reflection of automatic processing and WOULD FORCE THOSE OF US WHO HAVE ASSUMED that it reflects a post-lexical stage of comprehension TO RETHINK OUR POSITION.` A named observation, a design that would produce it (mask the target instead of the prime), and the authors' own position placed at risk by it. The corpus holds many predictions; this is a stated disconfirmer
span.quote: On the other hand, finding evidence of N400 priming effects on masked targets would strengthen the case for the N400 being a direct reflection of automatic processing and would force those of us who have assumed that it reflects a post-lexical stage of comprehension to rethink our position

span.label: A SECOND, SHARPER TEST IS SPECIFIED WITH ITS DISCRIMINATING PREDICTION: translation equivalents in bilinguals (arbre-TREE). `Modulation of the N400 by priming with translation equivalents SHOULD NOT BE SENSITIVE TO PRIME VISIBILITY since the same semantic representation would be PRE-ACTIVATED by the translation equivalent in the other language.` That separates the two accounts cleanly - a translation equivalent is semantically related but shares no form, so the form-versus-meaning account predicts it behaves like semantic priming while the pre-activation account predicts it behaves like repetition priming. The prediction is stated in the direction that would embarrass the authors' preferred story if it failed
span.quote: Modulation of the N400 by priming with translation equivalents should not be sensitive to prime visibility since the same semantic representation would be pre-activated by the translation equivalent in the other language

span.label: THIS IS THE STUDY THAT CONTROLLED WHAT Kiefer DID NOT, AND Kiefer2012 IS IN THIS CORPUS - tagged tonight, four records earlier. `NEITHER THE DEACON ET AL. NOR THE KIEFER STUDIES CONTROLLED PRIME PROCESSING and therefore it is not clear whether their participants allocated similar attentional resources to primes in their various conditions.` The go/no-go animal-probe task exists to hold attention on the prime epoch constant across durations, because otherwise a shorter prime is also a less-attended one and the two are confounded. So the corpus now holds Kiefer's gating account, this paper's methodological objection to the evidence for it, and both papers' own hedges
span.quote: Neither the Deacon et al. nor the Kiefer studies controlled prime processing and therefore it is not clear whether their participants allocated similar attentional resources to primes in their various conditions

span.label: contradicts → Brown and Hagoort
span.quote: The pattern of results observed in these experiments would seem to call into question the interpretation of the functional significance of the N400 offered by Brown and Hagoort [ 2 ] and others who have maintained that the N400 is exclusively sensitive to post-lexical semantic processes.

span.label: contradicts → Deacon et al. and Kiefer et al. reports of unconscious masked semantic priming
span.quote: Moreover, these findings draw into question previous reports of masked semantic priming that have claimed that the effects are due to unconsciously processed primes [ 6 , 14 , 15 ].

span.label: replicates → Misra and Holcomb; Schnyer et al.
span.quote: Like several previous studies [ 21 , 31 ], robust effects of repetition in the region of the N400 component were found for target words preceded by very briefly displayed masked prime words.

span.label: extends → Misra and Holcomb
span.quote: One limitation with the Misra and Holcomb [ 21 ] study was that their unmasked (identifiable) and masked (unidentifiable) priming data for immediate repetitions (i.e., the trials with the largest effects) were collected in different experiments in different participants.

span.label: repetition priming —contrasted-with→ semantic priming
span.note: differs in: WHETHER THE EFFECT TRACKS HOW WELL THE PRIME WAS SEEN. Semantic priming correlates with prime visibility across participants; repetition priming does not. Same measure, same design, so the difference is in the priming and not in the instrument - and on the authors' account it is a difference of MECHANISM (pre-activation versus establishing connections) rather than of representation · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE PAPER'S CENTRAL RESULT. Grounded on the sentence that states BOTH arms so a reader cannot take half of it, and the conditional `If we further hypothesize` is left in because the correlation is the finding while the resource account is the interpretation.
span.quote: If we further hypothesize that it is precisely the allocation of attention-demanding resources that determines the level of visibility of prime stimuli, then we can explain why prime visibility correlated highly with semantic priming and not with repetition priming

span.label: prime visibility —causes→ semantic priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.8 — WEIGHTED 0.8 AND `causes` IS DOING MORE WORK THAN THE DATA DO. This is a CORRELATION ACROSS PARTICIPANTS - nothing was manipulated between the people who saw more and the people who saw less - and the paper's own words are `likely played a role`, which is in the quote. The vocabulary has no `covaries-with`, so the note carries what the type cannot. No effect_direction: see the comment above this edge.
span.quote: This suggests that, unlike the repetition priming effects obtained in Experiment 1, prime visibility likely played a role in the semantic priming effects obtained at the shortest prime durations of Experiment 2

span.label: pre-activation —causes→ repetition priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.8 — THE PROPOSED MECHANISM, AND THE HEDGES ARE THE FIRST WORDS OF THE QUOTE: `One way to avoid this relatively ad-hoc assumption WOULD BE TO ARGUE`. This is the authors' preferred account offered as an alternative to one they have just called ad hoc, not a result. Weight 0.8 for that reason - it is the lowest-evidenced row on this record and the most interesting one.
span.quote: One way to avoid this relatively ad-hoc assumption would be to argue that the critical difference between repetition and semantic priming is that repetition priming is driven primarily by the pre-activation of representations that are shared by prime and target, while semantic priming involves, to a greater extent, establishing connections across related representations

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: Separate analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were performed using the within-subject factors of prime duration (short, medium and long) and repetition (repeated, unrepeated)

span.label: mixed-design ANOVA
span.quote: A mixed design ANOVA including a single grouping factor of Experiment (Experiment 1 vs. Experiment 2) and within-subjects factors as in the previous analyses revealed that, while there were no overall effects of experiment ( P values >0.5), there was a significant difference in the size of the priming effect between the experiments

span.label: t-test
span.quote: The mean of the high group’s d-prime at 40 ms was 2.1 which did significantly differ from 0 ( t = 9.2, P < 0.001).

span.label: correlation
span.quote: The correlation between target probe hits and 40 ms prime probe hits was not significant ( r = 0.03), suggesting that the tendency to detect probes in the prime position at short prime durations was not predictive of performance in the overall task of semantic categorization.

span.label: regression / coefficient of determination
span.quote: Fourth, across all 18 participants, the r 2 with 40 ms d-prime as the predictor variable and the N400 repetition effect at Cz as the dependent variable was 0.07 ( P = 0.30), suggesting no relationship between these variables.

span.label: d-prime (signal detection sensitivity)
span.quote: D-prime was calculated from the proportion of hits on trials with animal names in the prime position and false alarms on non-animal prime trials.

span.label: median split
span.quote: To help determine if prime visibility accounted for any of the ERP results (see below), participants were subdivided into two groups based on a median split of their d-prime scores in the 40 ms prime duration condition.

span.label: Robust N400 repetition priming appeared even for primes displayed too briefly to be identified.
span.quote: Like several previous studies [ 21 , 31 ], robust effects of repetition in the region of the N400 component were found for target words preceded by very briefly displayed masked prime words.

span.label: For repetition priming, individual prime visibility was unrelated to the size of the N400 effect at the shortest prime duration, arguing against conscious leakage as its source.
span.quote: Using several approaches, we found a lack of any apparent relationship between prime visibility and the size of the N400 repetition effect at short prime durations which suggest that conscious leakage had a minimal impact on priming at 40 ms.

span.label: For semantic priming, by contrast, prime visibility at 40 ms did predict the size of the N400 effect.
span.quote: So, unlike repetition priming in Experiment 1, for semantic priming in Experiment 2, visibility of primes at 40 ms (as measured by button presses to probe items) predicted the N400 effect for targets following very briefly presented primes.

span.label: Direct between-experiment comparison showed repetition priming produced a larger N400 effect than semantic priming.
span.quote: Specifically, repetition priming (Experiment 1) produced a larger overall priming effect than semantic priming (Experiment 2).

span.label: No post-N400 late positivity effect of repetition was found, even for clearly visible primes, unlike earlier unmasked studies.
span.quote: Unlike Misra and Holcomb [ 21 ] and a number of other previous unmasked ERP repetition priming studies (e.g., [ 24 , 27 – 30 ]), there was no clear evidence of an effect on the post-N400 late positivity.

span.label: The authors conclude that previously reported masked semantic priming effects were plausibly driven by conscious leakage on a subset of trials rather than by unconscious processing.
span.quote: A more likely explanation in light of the current findings is that these previous reports obtained their semantic priming at short masked prime durations because of conscious leakage on some percentage of trials.

span.label: masked priming
span.quote: Over the past 20 years, a somewhat different form of priming has been widely investigated, namely masked priming (e.g., [ 4 , 9 , 17 , 18 ]). In these studies, the prime stimulus is presented very briefly and is then immediately obscured by either a pattern mask (e.g., a series of letters or symbols occupying the same location on the screen as the prime) or the target word itself.

span.label: conscious leakage
span.quote: One question that dogs all subliminal priming studies is the issue of whether the obtained effects may be due to residual conscious processing of the primes on some percentage of the trials (a phenomena we will call “conscious leakage”) [ 4 ].

span.label: prime / target
span.quote: The first item, or “prime”, serves to establish some type of context and the second item, or “target”, is usually manipulated so that it either fits or does not fit into the prime context.

span.label: prime duration (40, 80, 120 ms)
span.quote: In addition to the two levels of repetition (repeated/unrepeated), there was another factor of prime duration (40 ms, 80 ms and 120 ms), which resulted in six types of critical trials (45 pairs/condition—see Table 1 ).

span.label: repetition (repeated vs. unrepeated target)
span.quote: Separate analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were performed using the within-subject factors of prime duration (short, medium and long) and repetition (repeated, unrepeated)

span.label: relatedness (semantically related vs. unrelated target)
span.quote: As in Experiment 1, there were two experimental variables: relatedness (related/unrelated) and prime duration (40 ms, 80 ms and 120 ms), which resulted in six types of critical trials of 40 pairs/condition (see Table 3 ).

span.label: mean target ERP amplitude in three latency windows (N400)
span.term: mean target ERP amplitude in three latency windows (N400)
span.quote: Mean target amplitudes for the same three latency windows used by Misra and Holcomb [ 21 ] were used to quantify the target ERPs in this experiment: 150–300 ms post-target onset, 300–500 ms post-target onset and 500–750 ms post-target onset.

span.label: prime visibility group (high vs. low 40 ms d-prime)
span.term: prime visibility group (high vs. low 40 ms d-prime)
span.quote: To help determine if prime visibility accounted for any of the ERP results (see below), participants were subdivided into two groups based on a median split of their d-prime scores in the 40 ms prime duration condition.

span.label: prime–target SOA held constant at 500 ms
span.term: prime–target SOA held constant at 500 ms
span.quote: with the variable post-mask blank screen designed to keep the prime–target SOA constant at 500 ms

span.label: n = 22 (18 analysed) — participants recruited for Experiment 1 (four later excluded)
span.quote: Twenty-two right-handed, native English speaking Tufts University students (10 male, mean age = 19.75) received $20 compensation for participation in this experiment.

span.label: 63% vs. an expected 23% — size of the 40 ms N400 repetition priming effect relative to the 120 ms effect, versus what conscious leakage alone predicts
span.quote: Fifth, across all 18 subjects, the size of the N400 priming effect in the 40 ms condition was 63% of the effect in the 120 ms condition across the midline sites, but based on probe categorization performance, the priming effect at 40 ms should have been only 23% of that at 120 ms.

span.label: 42% vs. an expected 25% — same comparison for semantic priming in Experiment 2, where the gap was not significant
span.quote: Across all 16 subjects, the size of the N400 priming effect in the 40 ms condition was 42% of the effect in the 120 ms condition across the midline sites, but based on probe categorization performance the priming effect at 40 ms should have been 25% of that at 120 ms.

span.label: r 2 = 0.434, P = 0.006 — relationship between 40 ms prime visibility (d-prime) and the semantic N400 relatedness effect at Cz
span.quote: This possibility was supported by the existence of a significant relationship between 40 ms d-prime values and the N400 relatedness effect at Cz ( r 2 = 0.434, P = 0.006).

span.label: 18% — proportion of masked animal probes detected at 40 ms, the authors' estimate of conscious leakage
span.quote: We acknowledge that our results in the 40 ms condition are undoubtedly contaminated to some degree by conscious leakage (18% of masked animal probes were correctly detected, suggesting that participants could sometimes consciously process primes at 40 ms).

span.label: ~1 µV (vs. ~4 µV previously) — difference in N400 repetition priming between masked and visible primes in this study compared with Misra and Holcomb
span.quote: Misra and Holcomb [ 21 ] found differences of approximately 4 µV between the two types of priming while the difference in the current study was closer to 1 µV averaged across sites.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cogbrainres.2005.01.003.
